title: Aramco Weighs $100B Gas-Unit Listing as Syria Becomes a Wartime Energy Corridor
subhead: Saudi Aramco hired Evercore to carve out a standalone gas division potentially worth over $100 billion, while Damascus began trucking imported gasoline into Iraq via Banias as Hormuz stays throttled. Brent climbed back above $105 as Trump rejected Iran's reopening plan and weighed a US diesel export ban.

sections.heading: Aramco Moves to Spin Off a $100 Billion Gas Arm
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco has hired investment bank Evercore to advise on a restructuring that would create a standalone gas division and open the door to a potential listing, according to Bloomberg News (via Reuters and The Star). Sources put a prospective valuation of the gas unit at over $100 billion — roughly three times the market value of Aramco's listed chemicals arm Sabic, whose shares have fallen more than 20% over the past year. Boston Consulting Group helped develop the plan under an internal effort dubbed 'Project Gamma', advising a split to unlock value. Aramco and Evercore declined to comment.

The timing matters. Aramco is trying to sell assets worth up to $35 billion to fund state projects and dividend payouts, and has been exploring the sale of real estate and a stake in its oil export and storage terminals. A gas listing would shift the company's growth story toward non-oil revenue at a moment when its crude exports face physical disruption. Growth in the gas business is centered on the Jafurah shale gas project.
sections.whyItMatters: Aramco is monetizing gas to diversify away from crude-dependent state revenue while Hormuz risk caps its oil lifeline. A $100B gas listing would be one of the largest energy IPOs ever and a signal that Riyadh expects the crude disruption to persist.

sections.heading: Syria Turns Into Iraq's Wartime Fuel Corridor
sections.body:
Syria said it has begun delivering imported petrol to Iraq through the Banias oil terminal on its Mediterranean coast, state agency SANA reported, under a renewable three-month agreement to secure energy supplies amid disruptions to Strait of Hormuz shipping. A Syrian Petroleum Company official, Ahmed Qubbaji, said operations started Thursday with a first batch of 57 tankers, with plans to raise truck crossings at the Al-Tanf border to 200 per day. Qatari firm UCC is buying the petrol from various global sources, with Syria transporting it for a fee. Up to 1,200 Iraqi oil tankers already transit Syria daily, Qubbaji said.

The arrangement builds on Baghdad's April decision to ship crude through Syria by truck after Hormuz effectively closed to Iraqi exports. Damascus, under authorities who ousted Bashar Assad in December 2024, is positioning itself as a regional transit hub, and the two countries are finalizing a contract to restore a key bilateral oil pipeline.
sections.whyItMatters: A land route replacing a maritime chokepoint is a concrete workaround the market can price. Iraq is routing around Hormuz at scale, reducing the export paralysis that has gripped Gulf producers since February — but truck-based flows remain far below pre-war seaborne volumes.

sections.heading: Oil Rebounds Above $105 as Trump Rejects Hormuz Plan
sections.body:
Brent crude rose more than 1% to $105.64 a barrel and WTI climbed to $93.11 after President Donald Trump rejected Iran's proposal to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Outlook India and Reuters. Iran presented the plan at the UN General Assembly, conveying it through Qatari mediators; Tehran's foreign minister said it would wait for an official US response. Trump told Axios on Sunday that he still expected US negotiators to hold further talks this week.

Prices rose despite recovering regional supply: preliminary Kpler data showed Middle East crude exports reaching 12.8 million barrels per day in September, the highest since the war began in February, with Saudi Arabia and the UAE lifting shipments. ANZ analysts cited continued Houthi and Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia as keeping regional supply flows vulnerable; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by Houthi forces early Saturday.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is now trading two competing signals: record regional export volumes versus rejected diplomacy and persistent missile risk. Trump's 'better deal' strategy keeps a ceiling on any price retreat, but the export recovery shows the supply system is adapting faster than the headlines suggest.

sections.heading: Trump Leans Toward a US Diesel Export Ban at $6.50 a Gallon
sections.body:
With US retail diesel at a record ~$6.50 a gallon, Trump told Fox News on Sept. 27 he is looking 'very seriously' at banning American diesel exports, warning it 'could drive up the price of gasoline for passenger cars a little bit' (Sedaily, NDTV Profit). The administration is split three ways: the president weighs an outright ban; Energy Secretary Chris Wright has floated voluntary export restraint; and refiners want a suspension of the federal diesel excise tax instead. NEC Director Kevin Hassett, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and USTR Jamieson Greer have spent the past week modeling a short-term ban.

The stakes are global. US diesel exports approached a record 2 million barrels per day last month as Washington became the supplier of last resort amid the Iran and Ukraine wars. A ban would hit allies including Brazil and the UK, which would have to scramble for fuel. Separately, India's oil minister Hardeep Puri said New Delhi will continue honoring its diesel export contracts despite any US ban.
sections.whyItMatters: A single US export restriction could export the diesel crunch to allies overnight. The real signal is divergence inside the administration — ban, voluntary restraint, or tax cut — with midterm politics and an autumn harvest driving the clock. The same refining shortfall is driving Europe toward its second energy crisis in five years: El Pais reported a quartet of disruptions — Hormuz throttling, Houthi expansion across Bab el-Mandeb, the earlier shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline (since resumed), and Ukrainian drone damage to Russian refineries. Francisco Blanch of Bank of America told the paper: 'there is neither enough crude on the market or, above all, enough refineries available to process it.' European governments are responding with tax breaks and subsidies (Daily Sabah), while EU energy chief Dan Jorgensen urged countries to curb gas demand.

sections.heading: India Facing 100% Tariff Threat Under Russia Sanctions Law
sections.body:
India is pressing Washington over the Graham Act-style sanctions law signed by Trump, which allows tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas — a list that includes New Delhi. Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri met a US Congressional delegation, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar about the measures, with India reiterating concerns (Reuters, The Hindu). Sources told The Hindu BusinessLine that a US trade deal could shield India from the 100% tariff.

The pressure lands as India is already pivoting away from Russian barrels, caught between discounted supply and US punitive tariffs. A former senior Indian ambassador publicly urged New Delhi to 'call the US bluff' on sanctions pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: The sanctions law is doing what military pressure could not: forcing India to reprice its Russian crude strategy. How Washington treats its largest 'strategic autonomy' partner will define whether the tariff tool works or triggers broader non-aligned pushback.

sections.heading: Critical Minerals: US Spending Billions, but China's Grip Holds to the 2030s
sections.body:
The Trump administration is pouring billions into building US and allied supplies of critical minerals, an effort Reuters and Seeking Alpha say is starting to show results while remaining structurally behind. Reuters reported that US reliance on Chinese rare earths will persist well into the 2030s even as Washington rapidly builds domestic mining and processing. Aerospace suppliers are testing rare-earth alternatives, reviving decades-old turbine coating formulas after supply disruptions from China.

New detail: US and Japanese officials met to discuss supply bottlenecks in Chinese yttrium — a rare earth vital to aerospace and chipmaking — two weeks before the Trump-Xi summit, according to a document seen by Reuters. In the US-China tariff truce, the two sides agreed to keep working on rare-earth and critical-mineral shortages. Australia's Hancock Prospecting, led by Gina Rinehart, took a $680 million loss on rare-earth bets this year, per the Australian Financial Review — a reminder that substitution is capital-intensive and financially risky.
sections.whyItMatters: Even with a tariff truce, the physical dependency is unresolved and the fix is measured in years, not months. The Hancock loss shows the private capital now required may not materialize fast enough to match the political ambition.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Investment Nearly Triples as Japan Bets Big, Korea Retreats
sections.body:
The Hydrogen Council's 'Global Hydrogen Compass 2026' reports cumulative confirmed investment in clean hydrogen projects grew from $47 billion in 2023 to $130 billion this year — a roughly 2.8-fold rise in three years, per Herald Business. Over 570 projects have reached final investment decision or entered construction, and operational clean hydrogen production rose 70% in a year to 1.7 million tons annually, with output expected near 3.8 million tons next year. China and Europe accounted for more than 80% of the net increase. Japan is committing 15 trillion yen ($95.2 billion) over 15 years, subsidizing the price gap for up to 15 years.

By contrast, South Korea — which imports 93.7% of its energy — is trimming hydrogen support even as the IEA argues hydrogen could reduce that reliance (Sedaily). The report notes that energy security is now rivaling carbon neutrality as the driving rationale for hydrogen investment.
sections.whyItMatters: Hydrogen's investment case has quietly shifted from climate policy to energy-security hedging — a framing change that keeps money flowing even where climate politics sour. Japan's decade-scale subsidy and Korea's cut show the divergence in national industrial strategy.

bottomLine: Monday's session was defined by adaptation under pressure. Saudi Aramco moved to unlock a $100 billion gas arm, Iraq routed gasoline through Syria by truck, and Middle East crude exports hit a post-war record of 12.8 million barrels per day — evidence that producers are building workarounds around Hormuz faster than diplomacy can restore it. Against that, Trump's rejection of Iran's reopening plan, his live consideration of a US diesel export ban, and Europe's slide toward a second energy crisis in five years all point the same way: the chokepoint has been replaced by a refining bottleneck, and the political tools on the table — export bans, subsidies, tariffs — are more likely to redistribute pain than remove it. Watch this week for whether US-Iran talks actually resume and whether Washington pulls the trigger on diesel.
sources: Reuters, Bloomberg News, The Star (Malaysia), Outlook India, Axios, El Pais, Daily Sabah, Sedaily, NDTV Profit, The Hindu, The Hindu BusinessLine, Arab News, SANA, Xinhua, Kpler, ANZ, Bank of America, Hydrogen Council / Herald Business, Seeking Alpha, Australian Financial Review
